title: September Unobligated Spending Analysis
text:
Data corrected on 2026-11-06



Earlier versions of the FY2018 to FY2025 data had four errors. Each workbook’s accounts were labelled with the first agency in it. Duplicate downloads and the DEFC workbooks repeated accounts. Allocation accounts were added into their parents. And total budgetary resources (line 2500) was called “budget authority”. All four are fixed, and this page was rebuilt from the corrected data.
On this page the yearly percentages barely moved, by at most 0.06 percentage points (2025: 1.24% before, 1.18% now), because the repeated rows inflated the unobligated balance and the resources together. The agency, bureau and account lists changed more. Before the fix, Military Personnel and Military Construction accounts were listed under Homeland Security, and the 2025 account outlier list had 20 entries, not the 13 it has now.

What the totals cover. The yearly summaries keep only accounts for which OMB’s report has both a line 2490 row (unobligated balance) and a line 2500 row (total budgetary resources). Accounts with no line 2490 row are left out. A few accounts each year have a line 2490 but no line 2500 row, and are left out too. So a total here is the total for accounts that report an unobligated balance, not for every account in the SF-133. Financing accounts are included. In FY2025 that leaves out 526 accounts, 147 of them with nonzero total budgetary resources worth $264.9B. The largest is 97-0040 Payment to Military Retirement Fund ($154.4B), whose raw workbook has no line 2490 row. The Hugging Face dataset keeps every account.

title: September Unobligated Spending Analysis
text:
2025 Outlier Analysis
An entity’s unobligated share is its September balance (line 2490) divided by its total budgetary resources (line 2500), for accounts that expire in that year. It is an outlier when its share is high against the others that year (z-score above 0, false discovery rate of 5%). Entities with resources below $100M (agencies), $50M (bureaus) or $10M (accounts) are left out. The “Higher Than Average” lists are the top candidates that sit above their own 2018 to 2024 average, or have no history.
